interest: Tracks Japanese official personnel in the U.S. in 1941, from tax exemptions to surveillance, departures and internment.
overview: This file consists of eleven pages of the Department of State's docket register and 'List of Papers' (purport sheets) for decimal file 894.01B11, titled 'Agents of Japan in the United States,' covering documents sub-numbered 298 through 373 dated between February 1941 and June 1942. The records systematically chronicle communications and administrative actions involving the Japanese Embassy in Washington, the Department of State, and the Treasury Department (Bureau of Internal Revenue) concerning diplomatic status notifications, federal income tax exemptions, and sailing permits for Japanese government officials, military and naval inspectors, trade bureau personnel, and academic researchers based on mutual reciprocity. The entries also illuminate mounting pre-war vigilance and wartime transition, documenting the closure of the Japanese Naval Inspector's Office in New York in August 1941, intelligence monitoring and investigations by the Coordinator of Information (William J. Donovan) and the State Department's Division of Foreign Activity Correlation in late 1941, the expedited departure of Japanese nationals prior to December 1941, and subsequent 1942 Department of Justice inquiries regarding detained Japanese personnel and reciprocal releases.

subfiles.about: A continuous eleven-page State Department docket sheet and list of papers cataloguing official correspondence, notifications, tax exemptions, and intelligence reports concerning Japanese agents and officials in the United States from February 1941 to June 1942.
subfiles.summary: This eleven-page State Department docket register (Form 1-207) catalogs papers filed under decimal classification 894.01B11 ('Agents of Japan in the United States'), spanning sub-numbers 298 through 373 from February 1941 to June 1942. The majority of entries record notes from the Japanese Embassy requesting federal income tax exemptions and sailing permits for Japanese military inspectors, diplomatic personnel, consular staff, and commercial or technical experts, cross-referenced with State Department certifications of reciprocity and Treasury Department instructions to collectors of internal revenue. It also chronicles key developments marking the slide into World War II and its immediate aftermath, including the official closure of the Japanese Naval Inspector's Office in New York in August 1941, pre-war intelligence monitoring by the Coordinator of Information and State Department correlation officers, and post-Pearl Harbor 1942 communications regarding detained Japanese officials and reciprocal exchange arrangements.
